entry.title: Federal Reserve terminates United Texas Bank BSA/AML cease and desist order that cited virtual currency customers

category.term: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

entry.content:
On September 4, 2026 the Federal Reserve Board announced the termination of two enforcement actions, both effective September 2, 2026: a Cease and Desist Order dated August 29, 2024 against United Texas Bank, Dallas, Texas, and a Written Agreement dated July 5, 2023 with Quontic Bank Acquisition Corp. and Quontic Bank Holdings Corp., Astoria, New York. The terminated United Texas Bank order (Docket No. 24-021-B-SM; Texas Department of Banking Order No. 2024-025), issued jointly by the Board of Governors and the Texas Department of Banking, recited that a May 22, 2023 examination by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and the Texas Department of Banking "identified significant deficiencies related to foreign correspondent banking and virtual currency customers, specifically risk management and compliance with applicable laws, rules, and regulations relating to anti-money laundering," including the Bank Secrecy Act, 31 C.F.R. Chapter X, and the AML requirements of Regulation H, "resulting in a compliance program violation." The order had required written plans covering board oversight, corporate governance, the BSA/AML compliance program, customer due diligence, suspicious activity monitoring and reporting, and compliance with Office of Foreign Assets Control regulations. The terminated Quontic written agreement (Docket No. 23-010-WA/RB-HC) was a savings and loan holding company agreement with the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia covering source of strength, capital conservation, a capital plan and cash flow projections. The Federal Reserve publishes terminations as a list and states no reasons for either termination.
Primary source: Federal Reserve Board press release, September 4, 2026 (with the terminated 2024 consent order, Docket No. 24-021-B-SM) — https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/enforcement20260904a.htm

entry.title: SEC transfer agent proposal publishes at 91 FR 56946 with comments due November 3, 2026; text asks whether stablecoins and tokenized deposits count as funds

category.term: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

entry.content:
The Federal Register published document 2026-18190, "Transfer Agent Rules" (Securities and Exchange Commission), a Proposed Rule, on September 4, 2026, at citation 91 FR 56946. The Federal Register DATES field reads: "This release was published in the Federal Register on September 4, 2026. Comments should be received on or before November 3, 2026." The published abstract states the Commission "is proposing to adopt new rules, amend existing rules, amend the existing form for registration with the Commission as a transfer agent (Form TA-1) and the existing form for reporting activities of transfer agents (Form TA-2), and rescind an existing rule governing registered transfer agents. The proposals are designed to modernize the rules governing registered transfer agents." The proposing release states that market participants "are actively seeking to bring blockchain-native, or 'onchain' transfer agents into the U.S. market, with some firms developing models for blockchain-based recordkeeping, tokenized fund administration, and cross-chain interoperability that would require transfer agents to maintain issuer and securityholder records on distributed ledgers." The release also asks: "Should the rule address whether stablecoins and tokenized deposits can be funds (in addition to cash) and whether the bank account could be a bank's custodial wallet?"

entry.title: FinCEN issues alert and trend analysis on digital asset investment scams run by overseas scam centers, citing roughly $12.7 billion across 33,904 BSA reports

category.term: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)

entry.content:
In a news release dated September 3, 2026, FinCEN states it published an analysis and an alert to financial institutions "to be vigilant to digital asset investment scams perpetrated by overseas scam centers." The release states that FinCEN analyzed 33,904 Bank Secrecy Act reports involving suspected digital asset investment scam-related activity filed between September 8, 2023, and December 31, 2025, "totaling approximately $12.7 billion in financial activity tied to suspected digital asset investment scams," and that individuals of all ages were targeted "across all 50 states and several U.S. territories." On typology, the release states that scam center operators use "guarantee marketplaces" to purchase illicit services such as online account creation, phishing and money laundering, and that "Professional money launderers integrate scam proceeds into the formal financial system through networks of money mules and through stablecoin transfers to digital asset exchanges outside of the United States." The release states that FinCEN has identified red flags to help financial institutions detect, prevent and report suspicious activity connected to scam centers, and encourages voluntary information sharing under Section 314(b) of the USA PATRIOT Act. The two documents are the FinCEN Alert on Money Laundering Activity Associated with Digital Asset Investment Scam Centers and the Financial Trend Analysis on Digital Asset Investment Scams 2023-2025. The release lists the affected financial institution categories as casinos, depository institutions, insurance, money services businesses, mortgage companies and brokers, precious metals and jewelry, and securities and futures.
Primary source: FinCEN news release, September 3, 2026 — https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-identifies-nearly-13-billion-linked-suspected-digital-asset-scams

entry.title: FinCEN reissues southwest border Geographic Targeting Order requiring MSBs in eight named counties to report cash transactions between $1,000 and $10,000

category.term: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)

entry.content:
In a news release dated September 2, 2026, FinCEN states it reissued a Geographic Targeting Order that "subjects certain money services businesses (MSBs) - which provide financial services outside of a formal bank - to enhanced reporting requirements with FinCEN." The release states: "The GTO requires MSBs to file Currency Transaction Reports with FinCEN for cash transactions between $1,000 and $10,000 occurring in specific ZIP codes in Bernalillo, Dona Ana, and San Juan counties in New Mexico, and Cameron, El Paso, Hidalgo, Maverick, and Webb counties in Texas. The terms of this GTO are effective for 180 days after publication on the Federal Register." The corresponding Federal Register document, 2026-18194, is a Rule titled "Geographic Targeting Order Imposing Recordkeeping and Reporting Requirements on Certain Money Services Businesses Along the Southwest Border," published September 4, 2026 at 91 FR 56776. The Federal Register abstract states the order requires covered money services businesses "to report and retain records of transactions in currency of $1,000 or more, but not more than $10,000, and to verify the identity of persons presenting such transactions." The Federal Register DATES field reads: "Effective date: This action is effective September 3, 2026." The order defines a "Covered Business" as a money services business as defined in 31 CFR 1010.100(ff) located in the covered geographic area, subject to a carve-out for any money services business covered by an applicable court injunction against the Geographic Targeting Order published by FinCEN on March 14, 2025 at 90 FR 12106.
Primary source: Federal Register, 91 FR 56776 (published September 4, 2026), and FinCEN news release of September 2, 2026 — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/04/2026-18194/geographic-targeting-order-imposing-recordkeeping-and-reporting-requirements-on-certain-money

entry.title: Five agencies issue joint statement that SAR confidentiality does not preclude banks from communicating with customers about suspicious transactions or account closures

category.term: FinCEN, Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA and OCC

entry.content:
In a news release dated September 2, 2026, FinCEN states that it, together with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the National Credit Union Administration and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, "issued a joint statement to clarify that confidentiality requirements related to Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) do not preclude banks from communicating with their customers regarding potentially fraudulent transactions and other suspicious activity or account closures." The release states: "This statement does not alter existing Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) legal or regulatory requirements or establish new supervisory expectations." The release further states that the joint statement "clarifies how banks can ensure compliance with SAR confidentiality requirements and provide customers with transparent and timely communication as part of the bank's fraud investigation." The release lists the affected financial institution categories as casinos, depository institutions, insurance, money services businesses, mortgage companies and brokers, precious metals and jewelry, and securities and futures.
Primary source: FinCEN news release, September 2, 2026 — https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-agencies-issue-joint-statement-suspicious-activity-report-confidentiality

entry.title: SEC proposes first substantive update to transfer agent rules since the early 1980s, citing blockchain use in share transfers

category.term: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission

entry.content:
On September 1, 2026 the SEC issued Release 2026-81 proposing to update the rules and forms that apply to registered transfer agents. The release states that the Commission's transfer agent rules "have not been substantively updated since the first rules were adopted in the late 1970s and early 1980s." SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins is quoted saying the proposal "would streamline and modernize the Commission's rules to reflect transfer agents' current processes and operations, including the use of electronic communications and blockchain technology in connection with securities offerings and the transfer of shares." The release states the proposal would amend existing rules and forms, would rescind a rule, and would introduce new rules applying to registered transfer agents and their activities. The proposing release is numbered 34-106246. According to the release, the proposal will be published in the Federal Register and the public comment period will remain open for 60 days after the date of that publication; as of this entry the proposal had not yet appeared in the Federal Register, so the comment period closing date is not yet fixed.
Primary source: SEC Press Release 2026-81 — https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026-81-sec-proposes-modernize-rules-registered-transfer-agents

entry.title: FinCEN section 311 special-measure proposal on Banque Misr UAE published in the Federal Register; comments close October 1, 2026

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury / Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)

entry.content:
FinCEN's notice of proposed rulemaking, "Proposal of Special Measure Regarding Banque Misr UAE as a Financial Institution Operating Outside of the United States of Primary Money Laundering Concern," was published in the Federal Register on September 1, 2026 (document 2026-17871, citation 91 FR 56085). The Federal Register record lists the comment period as closing on October 1, 2026. The published abstract states that FinCEN "is issuing a notice of proposed rulemaking, pursuant to section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, that finds the five United Arab Emirates-based branches of Banque Misr (collectively, Banque Misr UAE) to be of primary money laundering concern" and proposes a special measure to "prohibit U.S. financial institutions from opening or maintaining a correspondent account for, or on behalf of, Banque Misr UAE," to "require U.S. financial institutions to take reasonable steps not to process a transaction for the correspondent account in the United States of a foreign banking institution if such a transaction involves Banque Misr UAE," and to "require U.S. financial institutions to apply special due diligence to their foreign correspondent accounts that are reasonably designed to guard against their use to process transactions involving Banque Misr UAE." The underlying proposal was announced by Treasury on August 28, 2026.

entry.title: House Financial Services Republicans unveil the Consumer Financial Protection Accountability and Reform Act of 2026

category.term: U.S. House Committee on Financial Services

entry.content:
In a press release dated September 1, 2026, the House Committee on Financial Services states that Chairman French Hill (AR-02), Financial Institutions Subcommittee Chairman Andy Barr (KY-06) "and nearly all Committee Republicans unveiled the Consumer Financial Protection Accountability and Reform Act of 2026." The release states the bill "will restore accountability to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), provide clear and consistent rules for consumers and financial institutions, promote innovation and competition, and establish a more predictable, risk-based approach to federal oversight." On mechanics, the release states: "The bill brings the CFPB into the regular congressional appropriations process, establishes a dedicated Inspector General, and strengthens the transparency and rigor of its rulemaking process. The bill also requires periodic reviews of major rules to ensure their benefits justify their costs." It further states the bill "clarifies the Bureau's authority, strengthens due process, and establishes more predictable standards for supervision and enforcement," "makes clear that agency guidance is not legally binding," "reduces duplicative examinations and supervision," and "promotes proportionate penalties, rewards firms that self-report and remediate problems." Chairman Hill is quoted saying he looks forward "to bringing this legislation to the House floor." The release links the bill text, a one-pager and a section-by-section. The release does not state that the bill has been introduced, referred, marked up or scheduled for floor consideration.
Primary source: U.S. House Committee on Financial Services press release, September 1, 2026 — https://financialservices.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=411226

entry.title: CFTC settles insider-trading charges over prediction-market event contracts, ordering $172,000 and a three-year trading ban

category.term: Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)

entry.content:
In Release Number 9289-26, dated August 28, 2026, the CFTC announced an order filing and settling charges against Gabriel Perez for misappropriating material, nonpublic information obtained through his federal government employment in order to trade event contracts (i.e., swaps) on a prediction market platform for his personal benefit. Under the order, Perez must disgorge profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil monetary penalty of $65,000, which the CFTC describes as a substantial discount under the Division of Enforcement's new cooperation advisory because of Perez's cooperation; Perez agreed to cease and desist from further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC regulations, and a three-year trading ban is imposed. The order finds that between December 2025 and February 2026, while working as a teleprompter operator for the White House, Perez traded presidential mention market contracts, which are event contracts reflecting words or phrases the President may use during his speeches, generating over $107,500 in profits. The CFTC states that it appreciates the assistance of KalshiEX in this matter.

entry.title: FinCEN proposes a USA PATRIOT Act section 311 special measure to cut off Banque Misr UAE's U.S. correspondent banking access

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury (FinCEN and OFAC)

entry.content:
On August 28, 2026, Treasury announced that FinCEN issued a notice of proposed rulemaking finding that Banque Misr in the United Arab Emirates is a financial institution operating outside the United States of primary money laundering concern. Pursuant to section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, FinCEN proposes prohibiting U.S. financial institutions from opening or maintaining a correspondent account for, or on behalf of, Banque Misr UAE. Treasury states the rule would also require U.S. financial institutions to take reasonable steps not to process a transaction for a correspondent account in the United States of a foreign banking institution if such a transaction involves Banque Misr UAE, and to apply to their foreign correspondent accounts special due diligence reasonably designed to guard against their use to process transactions involving Banque Misr UAE. Treasury states the public comment period will close 30 days after the NPRM is published in the Federal Register, and that the finding and proposed special measure apply only to Banque Misr UAE and not to Banque Misr operations in any other country. Treasury estimates that between January 2024 and June 2026, Banque Misr UAE processed approximately $1.8 billion for 103 companies that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks. Separately, OFAC sanctioned Reza Mohammad Taeedi, described as the general manager of Bank Melli's Dubai branch, and Hong Kong-based Kameng Trading Limited, which Treasury states was used by sanctioned Iranian exchange house Pedram Pirouzan Exchange House to launder money for Iran.
Primary source: U.S. Department of the Treasury press release sb0617 (August 28, 2026) — https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0617
Relevant to: banks and money transmitters with correspondent relationships, payment processors, BSA/AML and sanctions-screening teams

entry.title: SEC charges 38 entities with using false Forms ADV to pose as legitimate U.S. advisory firms

category.term: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)

entry.content:
On August 27, 2026, in Release 2026-78, the SEC charged 38 entities alleging that they made material misrepresentations in Forms ADV filed with the Commission between 2025 and 2026 to falsely portray themselves as legitimate advisory firms to U.S. investors, and that a number of them used IP addresses tracked to foreign jurisdictions to connect to the Commission's filing system. Laura D'Allaird, Chief of the SEC Enforcement Division's Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit, is quoted stating that the complaints allege large-scale abuse of SEC adviser filings by persons, several of whom are likely located overseas, exploiting interest in emerging technologies. According to the complaints, the defendants listed places of business at addresses in Colorado where they had no presence, provided phone numbers that are disconnected or belong to unrelated businesses, disclosed ownership structures and numerical data identical or nearly identical to a multitude of other purported exempt reporting advisers, and claimed audits by one of two independent public accounting firms that cannot be found in any public registry of federal or state accountancy firms. The SEC also alleges certain defendants were marketed on websites, some displaying a fake certificate indicating SEC registration. The complaints, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado, charge violations of Sections 204(a) and 207 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The SEC states the ERA filings of the 38 entities have been removed from the Commission website, and that its Office of Investor Education and Assistance issued an investor alert warning that scammers are using SEC ERA filings to create a false impression of legitimacy.

entry.title: New York consumer alert on AI-driven investment scams names fake cryptocurrency projects and routes virtual-currency complaints to NYDFS

category.term: New York State Department of State, Division of Consumer Protection (published on the NYDFS newsroom)

entry.content:
On August 27, 2026, the New York State Department of State's Division of Consumer Protection issued an alert urging New Yorkers to remain vigilant against increasingly sophisticated investment scams driven by artificial intelligence. The release cites Federal Trade Commission data that 144,041 consumers reported losing over $8 billion to investment scams in 2025, a 38% increase from 2024, with a median loss of $10,560. Among the scam categories the alert enumerates are fake cryptocurrency projects, and among the warning signs it lists opportunities that require payments using cryptocurrency or wire transfers. The alert directs consumers to report cryptocurrency fraud or file a complaint against a virtual currency company in New York State to the Department of Financial Services. The release carries a statement from DFS Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow. The alert is educational guidance and does not announce a rule or an enforcement action.

entry.title: OFAC names the digital asset sector of Iran's economy in five new E.O. 13902 sectoral sanctions determinations

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury / OFAC

entry.content:
On August 24, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued five sectoral sanctions determinations pursuant to Executive Order 13902, covering the digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors of the Iranian economy. Treasury states that with the action OFAC "can now sanction any person, regardless of where they are located, that operates in" those sectors, and describes the digital assets sector as one where "the Iranian regime increasingly turns to cryptocurrency as a tool of choice for sanctions evasion, supporting transactions linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Iranian regime insiders." Treasury states the announcement "expands secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime." The determination document is published by OFAC as "Determination Pursuant to Executive Order 13902 - Aviation, Digital Asset, Gold, Shipping, and Technology Sectors of the Iranian Economy." The determinations were announced as part of what Treasury calls Operation Economic Outcast.

entry.title: Treasury launches a financial-sector Quantum-Readiness Task Force with a digital assets workstream

category.term: U.S. Department of the Treasury

entry.content:
On August 24, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the launch of the Quantum-Readiness Task Force, following Executive Order 14412. Treasury describes it as "a public-private initiative to help accelerate the U.S. financial sector's transition to quantum-safe technology in an orderly and operationally resilient manner," building on the G7 Cyber Expert Group roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography. Treasury states the Task Force "will operate through three workstreams: Sector Alignment & PQC Transition; Third-Party & Vendor Readiness; and Digital Assets and Emerging Technology Risk," and that future quantum systems "could break many of the cryptographic tools that protect financial data, payment systems, digital identities, and market infrastructure." entry.title: Washington court orders KalshiEX to stop offering sports, elections, politics, culture, tech and mentions contracts in the state and to geofence by August 19 and September 2

category.term: King County Superior Court, State of Washington

entry.content:
On August 12, 2026, King County Superior Court Judge John F. McHale signed an Amended and Updated Order Granting Plaintiff State of Washington's Amended Motion for Preliminary Injunction in State of Washington v. KalshiEX, LLC, No. 26-2-10264-3 SEA. The Washington State Office of the Attorney General announced the order on August 13, 2026. The order directs that Kalshi "shall cease marketing, advertising, promoting, conducting, operating, facilitating, distributing, offering, or accepting event contracts, or other contracts, instruments, or products in Washington, related to sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions," and states that this "does not include bets in the following categories, 'Commodities,' 'Climate,' Economics,' and 'Finance.'" It further orders that "By no later than August 19, 2026 Kalshi will implement IP address and residency based geofencing, and by no later than September 2, 2026, Kalshi will implement a multi-source geofencing solution provided through GeoComply," while providing that "Kalshi will not prohibit users from exiting positions they already hold." If implementation with GeoComply is not complete by September 2, 2026, the order states that Kalshi will either pay the State $120,000.00 each day thereafter until implementation is complete or submit a sworn affidavit explaining why implementation remains incomplete, with penalties in an amount to be determined by the Court if it finds insufficient diligence. The order also requires Kalshi to preserve records reasonably related to Washington consumers, including geolocation determinations and marketing and targeting data, to maintain the status quo as to transaction fees obtained from consumers who identified or self-reported as Washingtonians, and to provide Washington the same GeoComply implementation information it provides to Michigan and Nevada. On preemption, the order concludes that "The Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) does not preempt Washington State gambling law," that 7 U.S.C. 2(a)(1)(A) "does not contain express preemption language," that "while the CEA preempts the field of regulating on DCMs, it does not preempt the State of Washington's enforcement of gambling law under RCW 9.46," and that "The impartial access rule does not require Kalshi to violate state law," describing 17 C.F.R. 38.151(b) as a non-discrimination provision. It finds that the State has shown a likelihood that Kalshi's conduct violates multiple provisions of the Washington Gambling Act and that "Kalshi's provision, marketing, and advertising of illegal gambling activities constitute unfair and/or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce under RCW 19.86.020." The order records that on December 9, 2025 the Washington State Gambling Commission issued a notice stating that offering events-based contracts or participating in these markets is not authorized in Washington State, and that Kalshi is subject to a preliminary injunction in Nevada. This is a preliminary injunction entered on a likelihood-of-success standard, not a final judgment on the merits.

entry.title: CFTC staff advisory sets expectations for prediction-market incentive-program self-certifications
entry.content:
On August 12, 2026 the CFTC's Division of Market Oversight issued Staff Advisory 26-23, announced as Release 9282-26, reminding designated contract markets of their obligations under the Commodity Exchange Act and Part 40 of the Commission's regulations when submitting rule self-certifications for market-maker, liquidity, trading or incentive programs under Rules 40.5 and 40.6. The advisory states that staff have observed an increase in incentive-program rule filings relating to event contract products that are "procedurally or substantively deficient." It states that volume-based rewards with steep tiers or threshold bonuses "can encourage participants to trade solely to reach volume targets, heightening risks of wash-trading, pre-arranged trading, or other fraudulent, manipulative, or disruptive trading practices," that market-maker programs guaranteeing net profits or covering participant losses "may incentivize artificial strategies," and that "sweepstakes-like or randomized rewards programs or prizes based, in whole or in part, on pure chance, rather than pre-defined performance metrics, likely run afoul of Core Principle 2." A footnote adds that rewards "should not be offered through gamified, casino-style, or other chance-based mechanisms, including spin-the-wheel promotions." DMO staff recommend that all designated contract markets that have previously submitted incentive programs under Rule 40.6(a) review those programs for compliance and submit amendments reasonably within the scope of the advisory under Rule 40.6(a) or Rule 40.6(d) by September 14, 2026. The advisory states that it is informational, does not create new obligations, and represents only the views of DMO staff.

entry.title: DOJ announces Arms Export Control Act guilty plea in which roughly $30,000 in USDT was paid for export-controlled military communications hardware

category.term: U.S. Department of Justice, National Security Division

entry.content:
The U.S. Department of Justice announced on August 10, 2026, in press release 26-909, that Dingwei Chen, a 29-year-old citizen of the People’s Republic of China, pleaded guilty in federal court in Salt Lake City to violating the Arms Export Control Act. Sentencing is scheduled for October 19 and Chen faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. According to the release, Chen attempted to purchase military-grade satellite modems and radios manufactured for the U.S. military by American companies, hardware that may not be legally exported from the United States without a license from the State Department’s Directorate of Defense Trade Controls, which the release states generally does not issue licenses to export military goods and services to China. On the payment arrangements, the release states that after making an initial down payment of over $40,000 U.S. dollars, Chen and his co-conspirators switched to cryptocurrency, noting that “cold wallets are essentially anonymous bank accounts. Each transaction processed through them is private and untraceable,” and that they went on to pay roughly $30,000 worth of USDT, which the release describes as a type of cryptocurrency; the release states these down payments related to the purchase of 10 modems. The release further states that Chen worked with others in China to acquire the systems from foreign arms dealers on the black market, that the group discussed transshipment through Switzerland, pickup in Saipan and finally smuggling through Mexico, and that they communicated using an encrypted app through which Chen claimed the transaction was an initial deal and that he had funding to buy tens of millions of dollars’ worth of additional military equipment. The case was investigated by ICE Homeland Security Investigations and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and is being prosecuted by the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.

entry.title: FTC issues a policy statement that it will not pursue disparate-impact or 'unfair discrimination' claims

category.term: Federal Trade Commission

entry.content:
On August 7, 2026 the Federal Trade Commission announced "a policy statement clarifying that the Commission will not pursue claims based on disparate-impact or 'unfair discrimination' theories." Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson is quoted in the release: "Disparate-impact claims are nearly impossible to square with our colorblind Constitution. They impose liability for discrimination without any evidence that anyone intended to discriminate, which pushes businesses to make race-based decisions in order to avoid liability. The Commission never had authority to impose disparate-impact liability. Today, we announce that the Commission will never do so again." The FTC states that the policy statement follows a Presidential executive order on "Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy," and that the statement explains the Commission lacks the statutory authority to consider claims under this theory. On what remains, the release states: "The statement sets forth how the Commission will pursue discrimination claims in appropriate contexts. For example, it will continue to assert disparate-treatment claims under the Equal Credit and Opportunity Act, but it will treat Section 5 of the FTC Act as the consumer-protection statute it has always been." The FTC also states that under the new policy it reviewed past decisions based on statistical analyses designed to show disparate-impact liability and entered into agreements to modify certain compliance-related obligations for Napleton Inc., Passport Auto Group and an individual previously associated with Coulter Motor Company LLC. The release states the Commission vote authorizing the policy statement and approving the agreements was 2-0.

entry.title: FTC policy statement text: the Commission will no longer pursue disparate-impact claims in any context and will bring no antidiscrimination claims under Section 5, while the statement disclaims binding effect

category.term: Federal Trade Commission

entry.content:
The FTC "Policy Statement Regarding Disparate-Impact Claims and 'Unfair Discrimination' Claims," listed in the FTC Legal Library under date August 7, 2026, states in its Introduction: "The FTC has previously pursued disparate-impact claims in two contexts: under Section 5 of the FTC Act (where they have been styled as 'unfair discrimination' claims), and under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ('ECOA'). In both instances, the FTC acted ultra vires. Section 5 contains no antidiscrimination cause of action, let alone a disparate-impact one. And while ECOA does prohibit intentional discrimination, it does not authorize disparate-impact claims." It concludes: "Accordingly, in light of (1) the FTC's lack of statutory authority to bring disparate-impact claims and (2) the fundamental legal and policy defects of disparate-impact liability laid out in President Trump's executive order, the FTC will no longer pursue disparate-impact claims in any context. In addition, because Section 5 does not create an antidiscrimination cause of action, the Commission will not bring any such claims under Section 5." The statement identifies the order as "Exec. Order No. 14281, Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy, 90 Fed. Reg. 17537 (Apr. 23, 2025)" and says it directs agencies, including the FTC, to "deprioritize enforcement of all statutes and regulations to the extent they include disparate-impact liability." On what survives, the statement says "Intentional discrimination can be combatted through traditional disparate-treatment claims, and the Commission remains firmly committed to bringing such claims where the law allows," citing a July 17, 2025 concurring statement in the Asbury Automotive Group matter (Matter No. 2223135) stating the Commission "will not hesitate to bring disparate-treatment claims under ECOA where the facts support such claims." Footnote 1 states: "This Policy Statement does not confer any rights on any person and does not operate to bind the FTC or the public. In any enforcement action, the Commission must prove the challenged act or practice violates one or more existing statutory or regulatory requirements. In addition, this Policy Statement does not preempt federal, state, or local laws. Compliance with those laws, however, will not necessarily preclude Commission law enforcement action under the FTC Act or other statutes." The same footnote records that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated the Policy Statement as not a "major rule" as defined by 5 U.S.C. 804(2). The quoted passages are taken from the Introduction and the opening of Part II of the document; the remainder of the document was not read.

entry.title: FinCEN assesses a $125 million penalty against UBS Financial Services for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations, its largest ever against a broker-dealer

category.term: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), U.S. Department of the Treasury

entry.content:
On August 3, 2026 the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network assessed a $125,000,000 civil money penalty against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBSFS) for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. FinCEN states this is the largest penalty ever imposed against a broker-dealer for BSA violations to date, and that it is FinCEN's second enforcement action against UBSFS after a December 2018 consent order carrying a $14.5 million penalty that had also found UBSFS failed to adequately monitor foreign currency wires. FinCEN states that despite assurances it would remediate, UBSFS did not, and subsequently failed to appropriately monitor over 50,000 foreign currency wires with an aggregate value of more than $10 billion, and did not disclose these failings to FinCEN, which learned of them through an investigation opened after a regulatory examination. FinCEN also found failures to perform appropriate customer due diligence for high-risk customers with ties to Russia and Latin America, resulting in a failure to timely report hundreds of suspicious transactions. As part of the resolution UBSFS admits it willfully violated the BSA, including failing to implement and maintain an AML program and to file suspicious activity reports. The consent order requires UBSFS to work with a third party to complete a lookback for undetected suspicious transactions and to undergo an independent review of its AML program covering priority illicit finance risks that FinCEN identifies as the U.S. Southwest border, cartels and possible narcotics trafficking, Iran, Russia and Venezuela. FinCEN states it will waive up to $15 million for expenses incurred on that undertaking upon satisfactory completion. FinCEN states that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and FINRA cooperated on the matter.

entry.title: CFTC orders UBS Financial Services to pay $8 million for failing to diligently supervise AML transaction monitoring of foreign currency wires

category.term: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission

entry.content:
On August 3, 2026 the Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced, as Release 9277-26, a settled order against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBS FSI) in CFTC Docket No. 26-04, dated July 31, 2026. The Commission found that from January 2019 through June 2023 UBS FSI, a registered futures commission merchant, failed to adequately configure and administer its anti-money laundering transaction monitoring systems for wire transfers denominated in foreign currencies and effectuated through retail customer accounts, and thereby failed to diligently supervise its business in violation of Commission Regulation 166.3. The order requires UBS FSI to cease and desist and to pay an $8,000,000 civil monetary penalty within thirty days, and imposes cooperation undertakings. entry.title: SEC approves amended generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares, adding a 15% digital-commodity buffer and allowing actively managed products

category.term: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission

entry.content:
In three orders published in the Federal Register between July 30 and August 3, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved amendments to the generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares at Nasdaq, NYSE Arca and Cboe BZX. In Release No. 34-105995 (July 27, 2026; File No. SR-NASDAQ-2026-032), the Commission approved new Nasdaq Rule 5711(d)(iv)(C), which provides that up to 15 percent of a Commodity-Based Trust Share's net asset value in the aggregate may consist of digital commodities that do not meet the existing criteria for commodities, or securities that do not meet the existing criteria for securities, with any derivative calculated on its gross notional value. The rule defines 'digital commodity' to mean a commodity that is a digital asset and is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a functional crypto system, as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others. The exchanges state that this definition is informed by the joint interpretive guidance issued by the Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission published at 91 FR 13714 on March 23, 2026, and that each exchange will submit a rule filing to conform the definition if legislation is enacted defining the term. The same orders remove the requirement that Commodity-Based Trust Shares be designed to reflect the performance of one or more reference assets or an index of reference assets, which permits actively managed products to be listed under the generic standards, and add a trading-halt requirement where portfolio information is not disseminated to all market participants at the same time, together with a requirement that persons with access to non-public portfolio information be subject to procedures designed to prevent its use and dissemination. At least 85 percent of net asset value must remain in assets already permitted under the standards, and the Cboe BZX order states that the sponsor must monitor compliance with the 85 percent threshold daily and promptly notify the exchange of any breach. The companion orders are Release No. 34-106001 (July 28, 2026; File No. SR-NYSEARCA-2026-42), amending NYSE Arca Rule 8.201-E (Generic), and Release No. 34-106011 (July 29, 2026; File No. SR-CboeBZX-2026-061), amending Cboe BZX Rule 14.11(e)(4).

entry.title: CFTC staff advisory warns designated contract markets against broad, template-style self-certifications of event contract series

category.term: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (Division of Market Oversight)

entry.content:
On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Division of Market Oversight (DMO) issued an advisory reminding designated contract markets (DCMs) about the proper procedures for submitting self-certifications of an event contract series. The advisory addresses concerns about the practice of submitting broad, template-style certifications that combine many potential event contract variations into a single certification. According to the advisory, this approach limits DMO's ability to determine whether a DCM has provided all the information, explanation, and analysis required by Commission Regulation Section 40.2, and whether it has adequately evaluated the settlement methodology, data sources, and core-principles compliance of any contract it intends to list. The guidance reiterates that broad, template-style certifications should not be submitted, and explains when closely related event contracts may be certified as a class or submitted for approval under Commission Regulations Sections 40.2(d) or 40.3. The advisory was issued as CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-22.

entry.title: SCOTUS rules 6-3 that for-cause removal protections for SEC and CFTC commissioners are unconstitutional (Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332)

category.term: U.S. Supreme Court

entry.content:
On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court of the United States issued its 6-3 opinion in Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332), authored by Chief Justice Roberts, overturning Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). The Court held that the for-cause removal protection in the FTC's enabling statute — and by structural extension the SEC and CFTC, which operate under identical removal provisions — is contrary to the separation of powers under the Constitution. Effective immediately, the President may remove SEC and CFTC commissioners without cause. A companion order in Trump v. Cook (No. 25A312, June 29, 2026) denied a government application to stay a preliminary injunction protecting Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook; the Federal Reserve's statutory structure was not directly addressed by the majority opinion. The opinion is published on the Court's official slip opinion list for October Term 2025.

entry.content:
